title: The house that grew with the polder
subtitle: Over-Amstel, Binnenweg 17, Ouderkerk aan de Amstel · 1000 BC – 2026
notice: Unofficial educational reconstruction. Buildings before 1832 are reconstructed from the nearest excavated and surviving analogues; values tagged EST are estimates and REP marks documented stand-ins. Not affiliated with Over-Amstel Boerderij.
coords: Blender metres: +X east, +Y north (RD grid), +Z = m NAP; origin = BAG address point of Binnenweg 17; geometry in the 2026 height frame, lifted per year by zgroup curves; three.js (x, y, z) -> (x, z, -y)

systems.name: Roofs & thatch
systems.desc: Thatch, tiles, slates and zinc with their ridges, chimneys and dormers.

systems.name: Roof structure & frames
systems.desc: Rafters, purlins, anchor-beam trusses, posts and tie-beams: the timber skeleton.

systems.name: Walls & gables
systems.desc: Wattle and daub, weatherboarding, brick gables and façades. Each wall moves out on its own side.

systems.name: Doors, windows & shutters
systems.desc: Doors, shutters, leaded lights, sash and T-windows: they travel out with their walls.

systems.name: Interiors & fittings
systems.desc: Hearths and schouwen, bedsteden, furniture, dairy gear, stalls and painted ceilings.

systems.name: Floors, cellars & foundations
systems.desc: Clay floors, plavuizen, floorboards, cellars, post pads and the house mound.

systems.name: Strandvliet windmill
systems.desc: The farm's own drainage mill: wipmolen 1637–1722, octagonal grondzeiler 1722–1921.

systems.name: Pumping stations
systems.desc: The representative 1880s steam gemaal, the 1920s electric pump and the 1998 AGV gemaal.

systems.name: Boats
systems.desc: Log boat, punter, praam, trekschuit, tjalk, steamboat, rowing eight and the electric shuttle.

systems.name: Yard & outbuildings
systems.desc: Hay barracks, wells, fences, sheds, barns, paving, the garden and the jetty.

systems.name: Animals
systems.desc: Cattle, sheep, pigs, horses and poultry of each era.

systems.name: Dikes, sluices & bridges
systems.desc: Culverts, sluices, mill races, farm bridges, the road surface and bank revetments.

systems.name: Trees & planting
systems.desc: Alder carr, pollard willows, elms, ash, orchards, hedges, reeds and bog vegetation.

systems.name: Water
systems.desc: The Amstel and the polder ditches.

systems.name: Land
systems.desc: The bog, then the polder: today's survey heights, lifted back through time.

systems.name: Horizon
systems.desc: Churches, mills, the railway, the A2, the Bijlmer and the ArenA on their true bearings.

parts.name: The polder (1100 – today)
parts.desc: The reclaimed peat meadow of the Groot-Duivendrechtse Polder: the curved fan of ditches cut at right angles to the Amstel, the river dike carrying the Binnenweg and the farm terrace. Heights are today's AHN4 survey; three morph targets lift the meadow, the yard and the dike back to their historic levels, so dragging the year shows the land sinking about 3.5 m in 900 years.
facts: Drained peat shrinks and oxidises: about 1 m in the first century after reclamation, and still 4–5 mm a year today.
The ditch pattern is unchanged between the 1832 cadastral map and today.

parts.name: The wider polder landscape
parts.desc: Amstelland beyond the farm out to 4.4 km: Ouderkerk, the Bullewijk, Amstelveen and the edge of Amsterdam, from AHN4 at 40 m. It sinks with the meadow curve as one piece.

parts.name: Raised bog and fen (before 1100)
parts.desc: Before reclamation the farm's site is wet raised bog: a dome of sphagnum peat with heather and cotton-grass, sloping down to an alder-willow fringe and reed along a slow, dark peat river. The surface still grows upward until people drain it (about 0 m NAP in 1000 BC, about +1.5 m by AD 1000).

specs.Vegetation: Sphagnum, Calluna, Erica, Eriophorum; alder carr

facts: Amstelland was uninhabited peat bog until the 11th century; the only finds near the Amstel mouth are objects lost by passers-by.

parts.name: The Amstel
parts.desc: The Amstel at the farm: a natural meandering peat river about 56 m wide between two bends, kept at about −0.40 m NAP since the dam in Amsterdam (1265–75) turned it into a managed boezem.

specs.Centreline: ≈56 m west of the house front

facts: The towpath for the horse-drawn trekschuit (from 1599) ran on the far, west bank.

parts.name: Polder ditches
parts.desc: Water in the parcel ditches (kavelsloten) and the main drains (tochten), 0.3–0.5 m below the meadow. Dug at reclamation, they follow the meadow down as the peat sinks: by the 17th century they lie below the Amstel and must be pumped out by windmills.

parts.name: Front façade (west)
parts.desc: The four-bay front facing the Binnenweg and the Amstel: no front door, tall T-windows over four cellar windows, segmental rowlock arches and black wall anchors high up.

parts.name: South side wall
parts.desc: The yard side: one full window by the front corner, two narrower windows and, at the back, the entrance from the yard up to the bel-etage (the stoep and steps).

parts.name: North side wall
parts.desc: The north side, assumed to mirror the south (not photographed) [EST].

parts.name: Rear wall to the stal
parts.desc: The back wall, joined to the older stal by a 2.25 m link; a door at bel-etage level.

parts.name: Corner pilasters
parts.desc: Brick corner pilasters (lisenen) 0.54 m wide, standing 0.11 m proud on both faces, with recessed rustication bands every five or six courses in a slightly lighter brick.

parts.name: Frieze & crown cornice
parts.desc: A cream timber frieze carrying the name, under a profiled crown cornice projecting about 0.45 m; the gutter is hidden behind it.

parts.name: Front T-windows
parts.desc: Four tall T-windows: a cream kozijn with a fixed transom light over two side-hung casements, the sashes painted dark green. Grey stone sills.

parts.name: Cellar windows
parts.desc: Cellar windows as long described: the outer two blind (rendered panels), the inner two with vertical iron bars.

parts.name: Cellar windows (restored)
parts.desc: After the restoration all four cellar windows are glazed, in white frames.

parts.name: Mansard roof (shingles)
parts.desc: The flattened hipped (mansard-like) roof: steep slopes covered in dark grey-brown hexagonal shingles ('dakshingles'), zinc hip rolls and a zinc flat on top.

parts.name: Mansard roof (natural slate)
parts.desc: Re-roofed in natural blue-grey slate during the 2020–23 restoration, keeping the zinc flat.

parts.name: Chimneys
parts.desc: Two brick stacks with corbelled caps on the flat, one per front room's stove.

parts.name: Wide dormer (Amsterdam School gable)
parts.desc: A wide dormer with three pairs of casements and a small brick gable in an Amsterdam-School block motif. Historisch Amstelland judged it 'much later than the house'; present by 1958 [date c.1925 EST].

parts.name: Wide dormer (white pediment)
parts.desc: The restoration replaced the brick gable with a white classical timber pediment with a finial and two pointed consoles, framing the three window pairs.

parts.name: Floors & cellar
parts.desc: The bel-etage floor about 1.25 m above the front ground, the half-sunken cellar under the front rooms (later the Stams' cheese cellar) and the attic floor under the mansard.

parts.name: Name on the frieze
parts.desc: 'Over-Amstel' painted in black Gothic letters, centred on the cream frieze of the front.

parts.name: Oak log boat (Nigtevecht type)
parts.desc: A dugout hollowed from a single oak trunk, 8.6 m long and about 1 m wide, pulled up on the levee. Two transverse ribs were left standing in the hollow to stiffen the hull, as in the log boat found at Nigtevecht on the Vecht. Fishers and fowlers passing along the Amstel used boats like this.
facts: Oak log boat of the Nigtevecht type, 8.6 × 1.0 m (BRIEF.md S0; machines §3).
The Amstel 'slechts passanten': only passers-by, fishing and hunting; a bronze spearhead c. 900 BC at the Amstel mouth (Gawronski 2017) (early §1.1).
Hull depth and wall thickness [EST].

parts.name: Two leaf-shaped ash paddles
parts.desc: Two paddles carved from ash, with leaf-shaped blades: one lies in the boat, the other leans on the gunwale.

parts.name: Wicker fish trap (fuik)
parts.desc: A funnel-mouthed basket trap of willow rods on hoops, staked in the shallow margin of the river with its mouth downstream, for eel and pike.
facts: A wicker fish trap in the river is one of the justified human traces for the wild stage (early §1.3).
Form and size [EST].

parts.name: Camp hearth on the levee
parts.desc: A ring of field stones round a patch of charcoal and a few charred sticks: someone camped here a night while fishing, then moved on.
facts: 'A trodden spot with a small hearth': seasonal fishing and hunting fits the Damrak finds (spearhead, spindle whorls, 'passanten') (early §1.3).

parts.name: Fresh ditch end, spoil heap & spade
parts.desc: The head of a newly dug plot ditch: black peat sods cut out with the spade are heaped along the bank to drain and later to build the house mound. A wooden spade with an iron shoe is stuck in the heap.
facts: Cope reclamation: plots of 6 voorling (~1250 m) × 30 Stichtse roeden (~113 m) at right angles to the Amstel; ditch spoil used to build the mounds (Duivendrecht PDF §2.2) (early §2.1).
Oldest occupation between Diemen and Ouderkerk: end of the 12th c. (Gawronski 2017).

parts.name: House mound (huisterp)
parts.desc: The farm stands on a terp of peat sods and ditch spoil, capped with clay and raised by about 10-15 cm every decade as the drained peat sank. The sloping sides show the successive raising layers: peat sods, clay caps and trampled refuse. Two drip ditches along the house catch the run-off from the thatch.
facts: Oud-Diemen (3 km N): the mound was raised about every decade while the house stayed the same size; ten raising layers, late 11th–late 12th c. (early §2.2).
Sloten: plots raised on average every 10 years, nine superimposed farm plans (early §2.2).
Size after the Bovenkarspel huisterp, 12 × 25 m of peat chunks capped with clay sods (early §2.3).
Layer thicknesses and the 1:1.4 side slope are estimates [EST].

parts.name: Water in the drip ditches
parts.desc: Rainwater from the eaves standing in the drip ditches and the sod-lined well.

parts.name: Posts, tie-beams & rafters
parts.desc: Earthfast alder and ash posts dug into post-pits in pairs every 1.94 m along both long walls, joined by tie-beams and a wall plate. Couple rafters, hip rafters and hazel/willow laths carry the reed. The timbers inside are black with the smoke of two open hearths.
facts: Westerblokker: single-aisled, posts in the long walls in pairs about every 2 m, set in post-pits ('palen in kuilen') (early §2.3).
Alder and ash are the local timbers at Gouda-Oostpolder and Assendelft; oak only for door posts.
Post diameters are estimates [EST].

parts.name: Reed thatch with turf ridge
parts.desc: A hipped roof of Amstel reed about 36 cm thick at 50°, coming down to about 1.4 m above the yard. There is no chimney: smoke from the two hearths seeps through the thatch and escapes through small triangular smoke holes at both hip apexes. The ridge is capped with turf; the north slope is greening with moss.

specs.Smoke holes: ≈0.6 m gablets at both hip apexes

facts: Zaanstreek houses had 'wanden van gevlochten takken en twijgen en een dak van riet' (early §2.3).
No chimney before the 16th c.; smoke escapes through the thatch and the hip-apex openings (early §2.3).
Pitch, thickness and overhang are estimates [EST].

parts.name: South long wall
parts.desc: The yard-side long wall with the front-room door, a small shuttered light into the living room and, in the byre, a patch where the daub has fallen off and the woven wattle shows.

specs.Build: willow wattle daubed with clay, dung and straw, 15 cm

facts: Walls of wattle (willow/alder rods woven between stakes) daubed with clay, dung and chopped straw, about 10–15 cm thick (early §2.3).

parts.name: North long wall
parts.desc: The north long wall with the door into the byre end and one small shuttered light in the front room. Opposed long-wall doors as at Assendelft AsN-27 (early §2.3).

specs.Build: willow wattle daubed with clay, dung and straw, 15 cm

facts: Walls of wattle (willow/alder rods woven between stakes) daubed with clay, dung and chopped straw, about 10–15 cm thick (early §2.3).

parts.name: East (byre) gable
parts.desc: The low byre gable under the hip, with the wide byre door for cattle and dung.

specs.Build: willow wattle daubed with clay, dung and straw, 15 cm

facts: Walls of wattle (willow/alder rods woven between stakes) daubed with clay, dung and chopped straw, about 10–15 cm thick (early §2.3).

parts.name: West gable
parts.desc: The windowless west gable facing the Amstel, under the hipped end of the roof.

specs.Build: willow wattle daubed with clay, dung and straw, 15 cm

facts: Walls of wattle (willow/alder rods woven between stakes) daubed with clay, dung and chopped straw, about 10–15 cm thick (early §2.3).

parts.name: Wattle partition (living room | byre)
parts.desc: A wattle screen on the post pair at 10 m separates the heated rooms from the byre; a gap in the middle lets the warmth of the cattle in.
facts: Partition position from the Westerblokker plan proportions [EST] (early §2.4).

parts.name: Plank doors & shutters
parts.desc: Doors of split oak planks on wooden pivots in oak door posts: one in each long wall and a wide double byre door in the east gable. Two small square lights are closed with board shutters. A plank bridges each drip ditch at the doors.
facts: Two long-wall entrances as at Assendelft AsN-27; door sizes, byre door and lights are estimates [EST] (early §2.3).

parts.name: Clay floor, byre walk & gutters
parts.desc: Beaten clay over peat sods in the two heated rooms, strewn with reed and straw; in the byre raised stall floors along the walls, two shallow dung gutters and a central walk, a trampled mat of dung and straw. Each raising of the mound renewed the floor too.
facts: Floors of beaten clay, dung and refuse, renewed with each raising (Oud-Diemen, Sloten; Assendelft clay floors) (early §2.4).
Stall and gutter sizes [EST].

parts.name: Clay hearth plate (front room)
parts.desc: A slightly domed hearth plate of clay over packed sherds, edged with burnt orange clay, in the middle of the floor. A small peat-and-wood fire smoulders on it; the smoke rises into the blackened roof.
facts: Westerblokker had two heated rooms, each with a hearth ('haard'), and 'oranje vlekken met verbrande klei' (early §2.4).
Assendelft hearths were domed clay plates over layers of sherds.

parts.name: Clay hearth plate (living room)
parts.desc: A slightly domed hearth plate of clay over packed sherds, edged with burnt orange clay, in the middle of the floor. A small peat-and-wood fire smoulders on it; the smoke rises into the blackened roof.
facts: Westerblokker had two heated rooms, each with a hearth ('haard'), and 'oranje vlekken met verbrande klei' (early §2.4).
Assendelft hearths were domed clay plates over layers of sherds.

parts.name: Pots, quern & loom (front room)
parts.desc: The working room: grey-black kogelpots in and beside the embers, the imported Pingsdorf spouted pot, turned wooden bowls and ladles, a Rhenish basalt quern, stave buckets and willow baskets, and a warp-weighted loom leaning against the north wall with a row of clay loom weights.
facts: Kogelpots: hand-built, lens-shaped base, grey-black reduced fabric, sooted (ZH depot 14156, 32810).
The Pingsdorf tuitpot (references/era_1.jpg, ZH 41632, 1100–1225) with purple-brown iron-slip strokes.
Querns of Rhenish basalt lava are common on peat sites (Holland 2005 p. 246).
Spindle whorls at Assendelft and the Damrak; the loom type for rural Holland is uncertain [EST].

parts.name: Sleeping platforms & second hearth room
parts.desc: In the living room raised platforms along both long walls, edged with planks and filled with straw, with wool blankets: the household of about five slept here round the second hearth. No box beds yet.
facts: Raised sleeping platforms are an estimate: no excavated box beds this early [EST] (early §2.4).
Household of about 5 (Schokland study citing Brinkkemper) (early §2.6).

parts.name: Byre: 8 stalls (Friese stal)
parts.desc: Eight stalls in two rows of four, the small medieval cattle (about 1.1 m at the withers) standing with their heads to the long walls at hay racks, their tails to the central walk and its two dung gutters. Wattle hurdles divide the stalls.
facts: Westerblokker: a byre for 'maximaal acht koeien' (early §2.4).
Medieval cattle 108–115 cm at the withers (Gouda-Oostpolder; Holland 2005 p. 248).
Heads to the walls ('Friese stal'), documented for North Holland as far as Amsterdam (early §4.1).

parts.name: Open loft with hay
parts.desc: Loose poles laid across the tie-beams make an open loft over the byre and living room, stacked with hay, reed and brushwood. There is no closed ceiling: the soot-black roof is visible from below.
facts: Open loft over the tie-beams with hay, reeds and brushwood, no closed ceiling [EST] (early §2.4).

parts.name: Sod-lined well
parts.desc: A well shaft lined with stacked peat sods at the west end of the mound, with a wooden bucket on a pole hook. Westerblokker had one at each end of the house.
facts: Wells lined with stacked peat sods at Westerblokker (westerblokker_sod_well.jpg) (early §2.7).

parts.name: Wattle hurdle fence
parts.desc: A wattle hurdle fence on stakes round the foot of the mound keeps the cattle and pigs off the house platform and out of the kitchen plot; a gap on the river side is closed by a loose hurdle.
facts: 'Wattle hurdle fence around the terp' (early §2.7); height and panel length [EST].

parts.name: Dung heap & turf stack
parts.desc: Dung from the byre is forked onto a heap by the byre door, to be spread on the barley and oat strips. A stack of dried peat turves, cut from the plot for fuel, stands nearby.
facts: Dung pits/heaps by the byre door (Leidsche Rijn) (early §2.7); peat as standard fuel (early §2.6).

parts.name: Five-pole hay barrack
parts.desc: A hay barrack of five poles on a 7.3 m circle round a stack of hay, under a conical reed roof that rests on pegs through the poles and can be shifted up as the stack grows.
facts: 12th–13th-c. barracks: 5-pole Ø ≈7.3 m and 6-pole Ø 7.9–9 m, post-pits 0.45–1 m (Leidsche Rijn, Utrecht) (early §2.7).
Pole height and roof pitch [EST].

parts.name: Barrack roof (thatch)
parts.desc: The conical reed roof of the barrack, held on iron-free wooden pegs in the poles.

parts.name: Terp raised again (clay cap)
parts.desc: By the 14th century the old house mound has been capped with another layer of clay, burying the drip ditches of the first farm; the longhouse stands on it on brick pads.
facts: The old terp is now about 1–1.5 m high [EST] (early §3.2).

parts.name: Oak H-frames on brick pads
parts.desc: Eleven oak H-frames (gebinten) 2.2 m apart: squared posts standing on brick pads (poeren) clear of the damp floor, tie-beams with curved braces, wall plates, couple rafters and willow laths. Inside, every timber is black with two centuries of smoke.
facts: North Sea longhouse: posts 2–2.5 m apart, a tie-beam frame on stone pads (poeren) (early §3.1).
Pad and timber sizes are estimates [EST] (early §3.2).

parts.name: Reed thatch (hipped / half-hipped)
parts.desc: A heavy reed roof at 52°, hipped over the dwelling and half-hipped over the byre, coming down to about head height. The thatch is grey-brown with age, patched and green with moss on the north slope; a small smoke hole stays open at the dwelling hip and the ridge is capped with turf.
facts: Reed thatch 50–55°, half-hipped at the byre end, ridge 7.5–8 m, turf or straw ridge [EST] (early §3.2), after Rembrandt's langhuis drawing RP-T-1930-61 (c. 1652).

parts.name: South long wall
parts.desc: The yard side: wattle-and-daub in the dwelling end with two windows, then tarred horizontal weatherboards over the dairy (side door) and the byre (two small stall lights under the eaves).
facts: Byre and middle walls of horizontal weatherboarding, tarred; wattle and daub in the dwelling end for 1350–1500 (early §3.2).

parts.name: North long wall
parts.desc: The north side: the living-room door and one window in the daubed dwelling end, the second dairy door and one stall light in the boarded part.
facts: Opposed side doors into the middle house (Halbertsma '4'), an estimate for Amstelland (early §0, §3.3).

parts.name: West (dwelling) end wall
parts.desc: The dwelling end towards the Amstel, daubed and limewashed by the hearth, with one window, under the hipped end of the roof.
facts: Hipped or gabled dwelling end [EST] (early §3.2).

parts.name: Byre gable (vertical planks)
parts.desc: The byre gable under the half-hip: vertical planks on the end frame with a wide double door for the dung cart and the hay, as in Rembrandt's drawing of a langhuis with its hay barrack (c. 1652).
facts: Plank-clad gable and wide byre doors after Rembrandt RP-T-1930-61 (early §3.2).

parts.name: Doors & stall lights
parts.desc: Ledged plank doors: the living-room door on the north side, opposed side doors into the dairy, the wide double byre door in the east gable (one leaf open) and small shuttered stall lights under the eaves.
facts: Doors and openings per early §3.2–3.3 [EST].

parts.name: Shuttered windows (before 1550)
parts.desc: The dwelling's window openings, about 0.6 × 0.8 m, closed only by solid board shutters: glass is still rare on farms before the 16th century.
facts: Glazing rare before 1450; living-end openings with solid shutters (early §3.2).

parts.name: Leaded lights over shutters (from 1550)
parts.desc: From about 1550 the upper half of each dwelling window is glazed with small diamond panes in lead cames, the lower half still closed by a hinged board shutter.
facts: After c. 1550 the upper half has leaded diamond-pane glass, the lower half shutters (early §3.2; detail ref commons_archeon_achtertuin_middeleeuwen_2005.jpg).

parts.name: Clay floors, byre walk & gutters
parts.desc: Beaten clay in the living room and dairy; in the byre raised stall floors along both walls, two manure gutters (grup) and a central walk.
facts: Byre with 8–10 stalls, stall width ~1.1 m, depth ~1.7 m, gutter 0.4–0.6 m [EST] (early §3.3).

parts.name: Partitions (dairy | byre, early living | dairy)
parts.desc: A boarded partition with a door separates the dairy from the byre; until the fire wall is built a plank screen closes the living room off from the dairy.

parts.name: Plank screen living | dairy (before 1550)
parts.desc: A plank screen with a doorway between the living room and the dairy, before the brick fire wall.

parts.name: Open hearth on a raised slab (before 1550)
parts.desc: In the middle of the living room a fire burns on a raised slab of clay edged with bricks. A wooden beam across the tie-beams carries a notched iron pothook (haal) with the cauldron; smoke drifts up into the black rafters and out through the thatch.
facts: 1350–c. 1525: no chimney; open hearth on a raised clay/brick slab, smoke rising under the roof (agriwiki Schouw) (early §3.3).

parts.name: Brick fire wall & chimney breast (from 1550)
parts.desc: About 1550 the hearth moves to a brick fire wall between the living room and the dairy, with a brick flue rising to a stack through the ridge.
facts: c. 1550–1600: the hearth moves to a firewall with a smoke hood and brick flue (agriwiki Schouw); brick stack on a thatched Ouderkerk cottage, Rembrandt 1641 (early §3.2).

parts.name: Brick chimney stack
parts.desc: The brick stack through the ridge, with a projecting cap course.

parts.name: Smoke hood (schouw), mantel beam & valance
parts.desc: A wide smoke hood on two brick cheeks, with an oak mantel beam hung with a red cloth valance, as in Aertsen's Egg Dance (1552). Under it a brick hearth, a fire of peat and wood, and the cauldron on an iron pothook from the trammel.
facts: Hood 2.2–2.6 m wide on two side cheeks, timber mantel beam and cloth valance (early §3.3; Aertsen, Egg Dance, RM SK-A-3).
Cauldron on a pothook from a trammel (early §3.4).

parts.name: Living room: chest, bed, bench (whole era)
parts.desc: Things that stay all through the era: an iron-bound oak chest for linen and clothes, a free-standing bed with a straw mattress and wool blankets, a bench along the wall, a peat basket by the fire and wooden clogs by the door.
facts: Oak chest, peat basket, clogs (Egg Dance) (early §3.4).

parts.name: Living room things c. 1325–1550
parts.desc: Round the open hearth: three-legged stools, a board on trestles, red-glazed tripod grapen, a grey Siegburg stoneware jug and turned wooden bowls and ladles. The last grey kogelpots go out of use about 1350.
facts: Siegburg jug, grey-white salt glaze, 1320–1360 (ZH 6550); grapen from c. 1250; kogelpots common to the mid-14th c. (early §3.4).

parts.name: Living room things c. 1550–1575 (Egg Dance)
parts.desc: After the hood hearth arrives the room looks like Aertsen's Egg Dance: a trestle table under a linen cloth with a brown Raeren jug, pewter-like plates and a candle, turned chairs with rush seats, brass and copper basins hung on the fire wall, a spinning wheel and wicker baskets.
facts: Trestle table with linen cloth, turned rush-seated chairs, brass basins on the wall, stoneware jug (Aertsen, Egg Dance 1552; Kitchen Scene 1560–65) (early §3.4).
Raeren/Langerwehe brown salt-glazed jugs c. 1450–1600; a Raeren sherd of c. 1600 near Holendrechterweg, Ouderkerk (early §3.1).

parts.name: Dairy: milk tubs, pans & yoke
parts.desc: The middle house: shallow wooden milk tubs where the milk is set to let the cream rise, a shelf of pans, buckets, and the wooden yoke with two pails for carrying the milk in from the meadow.
facts: Milk tubs and shallow pans, buckets, the yoke with two pails (early §3.4); forms [EST].

parts.name: Plunger churn (karnton)
parts.desc: An upright oak stave churn with willow hoops and a plunger (dash): cream from the tubs is churned here into butter.
facts: Upright stave churn with plunger, H 0.9–1.1 m, whole era; the horse churn only from 1660 (Bieleman) (early §3.4).

parts.name: Cheese vat & lever press
parts.desc: A wooden cheese vat for curdling the milk, cheese moulds, and a lever press: a long beam pivoted in the wall, weighted with a stone, squeezing the whey from the curd. Holland turned to cheese for the market in the 16th century.
facts: Cheese vat, press with lever and stone weight, Ø ~35 cm vat (early §3.4); Holland turned to cheese for export in the 16th–17th c. (Bieleman).

parts.name: Byre: 10 stalls (Friese stal) & hay loft
parts.desc: Ten stalls in two rows of five, the cows facing the walls at plank mangers, standing on raised stall floors with the manure gutters behind them and a central walk. Over the tie-beams a loft of loose poles holds the hay.
facts: Friese stal: heads to the walls with a central walk between two gutters, the older system found in North Holland as far as Amsterdam (early §3.3).
Informacie 1514: Holland farmers kept on average only 4–6 cattle, more than 10 was rare (early §3.1).

parts.name: Four-pole hay barrack (kapberg)
parts.desc: Four tall poles round a square stack of hay under a pyramidal thatched roof that slides up and down the poles: iron pins through holes in the poles hold it at the height of the stack. Rembrandt drew exactly this beside a plank-gabled langhuis in a polder (c. 1652).
facts: Hay barrack with 4–5 poles and a movable thatched roof beside the house (Rembrandt RP-T-1930-61, c. 1652; RP-P-1962-86, 1641) (early §3.6).
Dimensions [EST].

parts.name: Movable barrack roof (kap)
parts.desc: The pyramidal reed roof of the barrack, raised or lowered on its four poles as the hay is stacked or used; the slider sets its height.

parts.name: Paling fence, dung heap, turf stack & kitchen garden
parts.desc: A paling of split stakes closes the yard towards the road and the south; behind the byre the dung heap steams beside a stack of peat turves; south of the house raised beds of leeks, cabbages and beans.
facts: Plank fence or paling, dung heap behind the byre, turf stack and small kitchen garden (early §3.6; Rembrandt RP-P-OB-471, 1648).

parts.name: Landing stage on the Amstel
parts.desc: A plank landing stage on oak piles where the farm's boat ties up: butter, cheese and peat go to Amsterdam by water (ferry from 1358).
facts: Boat landing with a flat-bottomed schouw/praam (early §3.6); waterways the main transport, ferry to Amsterdam from 1358 (early §3.5).

parts.name: Reed thatch (before the wing)
parts.desc: The long reed roof of the hallehuis, 50° with half-hips (wolfseinden) over both gables, sweeping down to about 2.2 m above the yard. Moss and algae grow on the north slope.

specs.Ridge: +8.58 m NAP (≈9.4 m above the yard)

facts: Reed at least 45°, preferably 50°; 28-30 cm thick at the foot (klavermakelaardij) [REF].
RCE: Amstelland hallehuizen keep a low-sweeping saddle roof or wolfsdak (half-hip) [REF].
De Haegh (1699, Dorpsstraat 1): afgewolfd thatched roof over a brick front gable [REF/PHOTO].

parts.name: Reed thatch
parts.desc: The same roof after c.1650, cut back where the opkamer wing rises through the south eaves.

specs.Ridge: +8.58 m NAP (≈9.4 m above the yard)

facts: Reed at least 45°, preferably 50°; 28-30 cm thick at the foot (klavermakelaardij) [REF].
RCE: Amstelland hallehuizen keep a low-sweeping saddle roof or wolfsdak (half-hip) [REF].
De Haegh (1699, Dorpsstraat 1): afgewolfd thatched roof over a brick front gable [REF/PHOTO].

parts.name: Ridge tiles
parts.desc: Half-round red clay ridge tiles (vorsten) bedded in clay mortar along the ridge, as on De Haegh today (17th-c. ridges may also have been turf; undocumented locally).

parts.name: Chimney stack
parts.desc: One brick stack over the hearth at the fire wall, rising through the ridge with a small pent cap (De Haegh); Rembrandt's farms show such stacks.

parts.name: Anchor-beam trusses, rafters & loft
parts.desc: The oak skeleton of the hallehuis: in the byre eight anchor-beam trusses (ankerbalkgebinten) on stone pads, with the anchor beams' tenons through the posts, knee braces, plates and ties carrying the rafters, battens under the reed, and the pole loft (sliet) for the hay.
facts: RCE: anchor-beam trusses, three aisles, central aisle wider and taller, harvest on a pole ('sliet') floor above [REF].
Bay spacing 2-2.5 m (polder_history Era 2) [REF/EST].

parts.name: Brick front gable (west)
parts.desc: The brick front gable facing the dike and the Amstel: red-brown hand-made brick in lime mortar, relieving arches over the windows, wrought-iron S-anchors, a loft hatch under the half-hip.
facts: Richer farms had a brick front house and a wooden byre by the early 17th c. (Agriwiki 7.1) [REF].
Red brick relieving arches and wrought-iron anchors (Agriwiki 7.1/7.2) [REF].

parts.name: South wall of the living part
parts.desc: Low brick side wall of the living part: a side door (to the opkamer wing after c.1650) and a window.

parts.name: North wall of the living part
parts.desc: Low brick side wall, mostly blind: the bedsteden stand against it inside.

parts.name: Fire wall (brandmuur)
parts.desc: The brick fire wall between the living part and the byre, carrying the hearth and the chimney; a door leads down two steps into the byre.
facts: RCE: the family lived and cooked at the front of the central aisle with the hearth against the brandmuur [REF].

parts.name: Front-room partition
parts.desc: A plastered timber partition between the woonkeuken and the voorkamer (front room), with a door.

parts.name: South byre wall (weatherboarded)
parts.desc: Horizontal overlapping boards (potdekselwerk), tarred near-black, on oak studs, with the achterhuis door and three ox-eye windows (De Haegh).
facts: Byre timber left unpainted or, for pine boarding, tarred with Stockholm tar (Agriwiki 5.0, 7.1) [REF].
RCE: after conversion small dung doors in the rear gable and a hay door high up [REF].

parts.name: North byre wall (weatherboarded)
parts.desc: The north byre wall: tarred boards, ox-eye windows and a door to the yard at the back.
facts: Byre timber left unpainted or, for pine boarding, tarred with Stockholm tar (Agriwiki 5.0, 7.1) [REF].
RCE: after conversion small dung doors in the rear gable and a hay door high up [REF].

parts.name: Rear gable (weatherboarded)
parts.desc: The rear gable after the Hollandse-stal conversion: a stable door, two small dung doors at the gutters and a hay door high in the gable for filling the loft.
facts: Byre timber left unpainted or, for pine boarding, tarred with Stockholm tar (Agriwiki 5.0, 7.1) [REF].
RCE: after conversion small dung doors in the rear gable and a hay door high up [REF].

parts.name: Front windows & door
parts.desc: Two oak cross-mullion windows (kruiskozijnen) in Bentheimer off-white: leaded lights above, leaded casements behind red shutters below; a front door used only for weddings and funerals; a loft hatch.

specs.Colours: frames Bentheimer, shutters red (red ochre inside)

facts: Kruiskozijnen in farms into the 17th c.; upper lights leaded glass, lower lights shutters (Agriwiki Kruiskozijn) [REF].
Shutters red / slate / yellowish outside, red ochre inside; frames Bentheimer or slate grey (Agriwiki 7.2) [REF].

parts.name: Side windows & doors (living part)
parts.desc: Smaller cross windows in the low side walls and the side door, slate-grey and yellowish shutters.

parts.name: Byre doors & ox-eye windows
parts.desc: Ox-eye windows (ossenogen) and split doors in the tarred byre walls; dung doors and the hay door in the rear gable.

parts.name: Plavuizen floor (living part)
parts.desc: Red and blue-smoked clay floor tiles (plavuizen) in a paired pattern, with fine white sand strewn in waves and rosettes on Saturdays.
facts: Floors of red or blue-smoked plavuizen, sometimes patterned (Agriwiki 9.1) [REF].
Sand strewn in patterns on Saturdays, described by Huygens (Agriwiki 9.5) [REF].

parts.name: Brick footings
parts.desc: Brick strip footings under the walls and a clay bed under the floors.

parts.name: Byre floor & gutters
parts.desc: Clay byre floor with the two dung gutters (grups, 0.4 × 0.25 m) behind the stands and a raised brick feed passage.
facts: Hollandse stal: grup ≈0.4 m wide × 0.2-0.3 m deep; clay floor (Agriwiki Grupstal, 9.2) [REF/EST].

parts.name: Ceiling joists & loft floor
parts.desc: Exposed ceiling joists and boards over the living part; in the byre the pole floor (sliet) on the anchor beams.

parts.name: Open hearth & schouw
parts.desc: The open hearth on the floor against the fire wall: a brick hearthstone between two plastered cheeks, a straight hood (rookvang) with an oak mantel shelf of pewter and Delftware, a cast-iron fire-back, a peat fire, and a cauldron on an iron pothook (haal) from a swinging crane; candles in niches.
facts: Schouw: open hearth on the floor against the brandmuur with a brick hood and schouwlijst, carried by cheeks in the 16th-17th c.; old schouwen may have candle niches (Agriwiki Schouw) [REF].
Peat (turf) was the hearth fuel [EST]; pothook, fire-back, cauldrons and grapen are standard Holland inventory items seen in Ostade and De Hooch [EST].

parts.name: Wall tiles beside the soot band
parts.desc: From c.1650 white tiles with blue figures and ox-head corner motifs line the fire wall beside the dark soot band and the inner faces of the cheeks (13 cm tiles).
facts: From c.1650 more (mainly white) tiles beside the dark soot band of the hearth (Agriwiki 9.1/9.3) [REF].
Figure tile with a churning woman and ox-head corner motif, 1625-1650 (Museum Rotterdam 17266) [REF]; 13 × 13 cm format [EST].

parts.name: Woonkeuken furniture
parts.desc: The living kitchen: two curtained bedsteden with a cupboard (spinde) between against the north wall, an oak table with rush-seated ladder-back chairs, an oak kussenkast, a plate rack with pewter and Delftware, a spinning wheel by the hearth, a foot-warmer and candles.
facts: Bedsteden 1.10-1.20 × 1.50-1.90 m, closed by curtains not reaching the floor (17th c.), with a spinde between (Agriwiki Bedstede) [REF].
Ladder-back chairs with rush seats, kussenkast, plate rack, voetstoof: Holland inventory items [EST].

parts.name: Front room (cheese store)
parts.desc: The front room, in Holland butter-and-cheese farms often a cheese store (kaaskamer): racks of cheeses on boards, a chest and a chair.
facts: In South-Holland butter/cheese farms the voorkamer doubled as a cheese store (Agriwiki Melkkelder) [REF].

parts.name: Hollandse stal fittings
parts.desc: Twenty cows stood in two rows heading to the central feed passage: wooden troughs, stall posts and partitions every two stands, tethering rings; a horse stall and a calf pen at the back; a horn lantern.
facts: RCE: the Hollandse stal turned the cows' heads to a central feed passage, with dung gutters along the side walls [REF].
Second half of the 17th c.: 18-25 cattle per South-Holland farm (Bieleman, Een land van vee) [REF].

parts.name: Hay on the loft
parts.desc: Meadow hay stacked on the sliet up into the roof.

parts.name: Opkamer wing roof
parts.desc: The thatched roof of the opkamer wing, its ridge at right angles to the main roof, its valley running into the south slope.
facts: RCE: a sunken milk cellar with an opkamer above was added; sideways on one side = krukhuis [REF].
Opkamer floor 3-5 steps above the house floor; cellar about half below ground (Agriwiki Opkamer) [REF]; here the cellar sits only 0.33 m below the house floor because today's ground is used [EST].

parts.name: Opkamer wing walls
parts.desc: Brick walls of the krukhuis wing: the gable faces south, the low cellar windows sit at ground level under the raised opkamer windows (De Haegh, krukhuis Ouderkerk 1966).
facts: RCE: a sunken milk cellar with an opkamer above was added; sideways on one side = krukhuis [REF].
Opkamer floor 3-5 steps above the house floor; cellar about half below ground (Agriwiki Opkamer) [REF]; here the cellar sits only 0.33 m below the house floor because today's ground is used [EST].

parts.name: Limewash band
parts.desc: From the second half of the 17th c. the base of the brick front was limewashed every year, from about one metre up to reaching height, stepping at the corners.
facts: Lower façade limewashed yearly from c.1650, about 1 m up to reaching height (Agriwiki 7.2) [REF].

parts.name: Opkamer & cellar windows
parts.desc: Raised opkamer windows with slate-grey shutters; low cellar windows without glass, with close wooden bars against cats, two iron bars and inner shutters, opened at night for cool air.
facts: Milk-cellar windows: unglazed, inner and outer shutters, one or two iron bars and close wooden bars against cats; opened at night (Agriwiki Melkkelder) [REF].

parts.name: Cellar floor, stairs & opkamer floor
parts.desc: Red plavuizen in the milk cellar, a landing and steps from the woonkeuken door down into the cellar and up to the opkamer; the opkamer has a pine board floor on oak joists.

parts.name: Milk cellar
parts.desc: The cool half-sunken milk cellar: shallow earthenware milk dishes on brick benches for the cream to rise, a plunger churn, the curdling tub, cheese moulds, a lever cheese press and pails.
facts: Milk set in large shallow dishes for the cream to rise; skimmed cream churned to butter (Agriwiki Melkkelder) [REF].
Kaaskuip, kaasvaten, lever press, cheese boards: standard Holland dairy kit; HA mentions old wooden cheese vats, a press and a butter churn [REF/EST].

parts.name: Opkamer (best room)
parts.desc: The opkamer over the cellar: pine floor, a pine wainscot band, a walnut two-part cabinet (kabinet), a mirror, a table and chairs: the best room, where guests and the owner from Amsterdam stayed.
facts: Opkamer: pine floor, panelling, best furniture such as a kabinet, mirror and painted chests (Agriwiki Opkamer, 9.1) [REF].
Amsterdam institutions and citizens owned Amstelland farms (Bouwlust before 1758; Strandvlied bought 1682) [REF HA].

parts.name: Kapberg poles & floor
parts.desc: The free-standing hay barrack (kapberg): four oak poles (roeden) 7.5 m tall and 4.9 m apart, drilled with rows of holes for the iron pins that hold the roof, on a low timber floor.
facts: Four-pole hooiberg: the most common type in the Netherlands; roof raised with a lever or barn winch and held by iron pins in the pole holes (pape-hooiberg, Hooidelta) [REF].
RCE: when the loft was too small a free-standing kapberg with a height-adjustable roof was built [REF].
Rembrandt B225 (1641) and Van Goyen (1628) show such barracks [REF].

parts.name: Hay in the kapberg
parts.desc: Loose meadow hay stacked under the kap.

parts.name: Kapberg roof (movable kap)
parts.desc: The reed-thatched pyramidal roof (kap) on a square timber frame. It slides up and down the four poles and rests on iron pins pushed through the pole holes: raised as the hay stack grows, lowered as it is used. Modelled at its lowest position; the viewer slider lifts it up to 4.5 m.
facts: The kap is held by iron pins in holes in the poles and raised with a lever, ratchet or barn winch (Hooidelta: heffen en bewegen van de kap) [REF].

parts.name: Dung heap (mestvaalt)
parts.desc: The dung heap behind the byre at the dung doors, mucked out from the gutters every day.
facts: Dung heap (mestvaalt) behind the byre at the dung doors (Agriwiki Grupstal); visible at Bouwlust 1958 [REF/PHOTO].

parts.name: Turf stack
parts.desc: A stack of dried peat (turf), the hearth fuel, built in courses under a ridge.

parts.name: Kitchen garden
parts.desc: The kitchen garden south of the house: beds of cabbage, beans on poles and onions, behind a white board paling like Rembrandt's 'Cottage with a White Paling' (1648).
facts: White paling (vertical boards) round the yard: Rembrandt B232, 1648 [REF].
Kitchen garden with cabbage, beans and onions [EST].

parts.name: Board fence
parts.desc: Tarred board fence along the north and east edge of the farmyard.
facts: Board fences round the yard (Rembrandt; 1752 drawing RP-T-1899-A-4175) [REF].

parts.name: Wooden pump
parts.desc: A wooden pump (houten pomp) with an iron handle over a stone trough, by the achterhuis door: water for the dairy gear and the cattle.

parts.name: Stal walls
parts.desc: The low brick walls of the stal that is older than the voorhuis (BAG 1889), about 2.85 m from floor to eaves, with half-hipped gables. Small-paned white windows and one blocked arched window [REF HA; PHOTO ha_1958_a, ha_stal_2016].

parts.name: Stal roof (dark tiles)
parts.desc: Half-hipped saddle roof covered in dark grey-black pantiles on boarding, as in the 1958 photographs [REF HA 'afgewolfd zadeldak'; PHOTO ha_1958_a, ha_main].

parts.name: Stal roof, holed and tarpaulined
parts.desc: By 2014 the roof was 'gatenkaas', full of holes, patched with tarpaulins weighted down with bricks [REF AEN 2014]. Mossy tiles, holes over the standings, three tarps.

parts.name: Stal roof (restored, roof lights)
parts.desc: Re-roofed in dark tiles during the 2020–23 restoration, with roof lights over the restaurant [PHOTO oa_barn_yard_cheese_store; REF QT].

parts.name: Stal roof timbers
parts.desc: Rafters at about 0.9 m on a ridge beam and two purlins per side, hip rafters at the half-hips; the boarding is nailed on top. Exposed (and limewash-free) in the restaurant [EST, PHOTO qt_restaurant].

parts.name: Stal windows
parts.desc: Small-paned white windows under segmental arches, as on the 1958 photograph of the stal behind the house [PHOTO ha_1958_a]; kept and reglazed in the restoration.

parts.name: Stal doors (boarded)
parts.desc: Ledged-and-braced board doors: the double barn door on the north side, the dung doors in the east gable through which the manure was barrowed out to the praam in the ditch [REF AEN] and the door to the link [EST].

parts.name: Glazed barn door
parts.desc: The barn door opening re-made as a large steel-framed glazed door looking out over the polder [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior].

parts.name: Link to the voorhuis
parts.desc: The 2.25 m deep link between the back wall of the 1894 voorhuis and the older stal: a flat-roofed brick passage with stairs from the bel-etage door down to the stal floor, about 2 m lower [MEAS BAG; layout EST].

parts.name: Neck and flat-roofed block
parts.desc: East of the stal a 4.7 × 3.9 m neck leads to an 8.4 × 8.4 m flat-roofed brick block, roof about +2.3 m NAP. Its use is undocumented: modelled as the milk and machine room of the machine-milking era (bulk tank from c.1975) [MEAS BAG/AHN; date and use EST].

parts.name: Stal floor (standings, gutters, passage)
parts.desc: Brick-paved feed passage down the middle, the cows' standings either side and the manure gutters (grup) behind them, then walkways along the walls [PHOTO ha_stal_2016; layout EST: Hollandse stal].

parts.name: Restaurant floor (reclaimed brick)
parts.desc: Reclaimed brick pavers laid in stretcher and herringbone bands, with a smooth screed aisle along the bar [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior; REF QT 'a brick floor'].

parts.name: Limewashed stal walls
parts.desc: Brick walls limewashed white inside, renewed every spring for hygiene [PHOTO ha_stal_2016; EST].

parts.name: Peeling limewash
parts.desc: Peeling, green-stained limewash after the herd left [PHOTO ha_stal_2016].

parts.name: Warm-grey render
parts.desc: Rendered and limewashed in a warm grey for the restaurant [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior].

parts.name: Tie beams
parts.desc: Tie beams across the stal at every post bay, carried by the side walls and the two post rows [PHOTO ha_stal_2016]; kept (and partly renewed in oak) for the restaurant [PHOTO qt_restaurant].

parts.name: Hay loft
parts.desc: Boarded hay loft over the stal, with loose hay and straw stored above the cows [PHOTO ha_stal_2016; REF QT 'hayloft'].

parts.name: Hay on the loft
parts.desc: Hay stacked under the roof for the winter [EST].

parts.name: Posts on stone pedestals
parts.desc: Rough round posts (about 25 cm) on stone pedestals carrying the loft, between trough and standings [PHOTO ha_stal_2016].

parts.name: Stone feed trough with pump
parts.desc: 'The nineteenth-century stone feed trough with water pump' still in the old stal in 2014: maize, linseed meal and pulp were mixed here with water pumped from the Amstel into 'slobber' [REF AEN].

parts.name: Timber feed troughs
parts.desc: Plank feed troughs along both sides of the feed passage in the hand-milking stal [EST].

parts.name: Neck chains
parts.desc: Chain neck tethers hanging from the beams, one per cow [PHOTO ha_stal_2016].

parts.name: Hand-milking gear
parts.desc: Milking stools and wooden pails by the standings, a stable lantern on a post: cows were milked by hand twice a day [REF AEN; props scanned, EST placement].

parts.name: Concrete feed troughs
parts.desc: Cast concrete feed troughs (voergoot) along the passage [PHOTO ha_stal_2016; date EST].

parts.name: Milking-machine pipeline
parts.desc: A galvanised vacuum/milk pipeline (pipeleiding) along under the beams with a tap at every pair of cows: machine milking replaced hand milking in the 1950s [PHOTO ha_stal_2016; date EST].

parts.name: Drinking bowls
parts.desc: Cast-iron automatic drinking bowls on the post pedestals, one between two cows [PHOTO ha_stal_2016].

parts.name: Electric stable lamps
parts.desc: Bare bulbs in enamel shades on the beams once the farm was on the grid (poles by 1958) [EST].

parts.name: Milking-machine units
parts.desc: Stainless bucket milking units with pulsator lids, carried from cow to cow and plugged into the vacuum line [EST typical 1950s–70s].

parts.name: Straw and debris
parts.desc: After the herd went to Friesland in 2013 the stal stood empty: old straw over the standings, a fallen board, a rusted barrow [PHOTO ha_stal_2016].

parts.name: Oak posts and braces
parts.desc: New sawn oak posts with pegged knee braces under the tie beams of the restaurant [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior, vr_2025_collage].

parts.name: Long oak tables
parts.desc: Long plank tables of solid oak, about 1 × 4 m, on heavy oak trestles, laid with white napkins, glasses and cordless candle lamps [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior].

parts.name: Candle lamps
parts.desc: Warm table lamps along the tables and over the bar [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior].

parts.name: Open kitchen and bar
parts.desc: A black steel bar and open kitchen along the south wall: back counter with the hob line and hood, bottles, a brass espresso machine [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior; REF MH].

parts.name: Wood fire
parts.desc: An open wood fire in a black steel hearth with a flue through the roof, at the west end [PHOTO oa_restaurant_table_fire; position EST].

parts.name: Hay bales and hayloft
parts.desc: Hay bales as decoration by the glazed door and on a short hayloft over the east end [PHOTO qt_restaurant_interior; REF QT 'hayloft'].

parts.name: Ground at the mill site before the polder mill
parts.desc: The ground round the mill at 1-2 m (0.5 m by the mill) with wall-aligned cuts for the race, the wheel pit, the screw trench and the board-lined voorwaterloop, so the water works show. It replaces the 5 m terrain lattice here (147 lattice quads cut) and subsides with the meadow.

parts.name: Molenerf with the wipmolen race and the voorwaterloop
parts.desc: The ground round the mill at 1-2 m (0.5 m by the mill) with wall-aligned cuts for the race, the wheel pit, the screw trench and the board-lined voorwaterloop, so the water works show. It replaces the 5 m terrain lattice here (147 lattice quads cut) and subsides with the meadow.

parts.name: Molenerf with the scoop-wheel race and the voorwaterloop
parts.desc: The ground round the mill at 1-2 m (0.5 m by the mill) with wall-aligned cuts for the race, the wheel pit, the screw trench and the board-lined voorwaterloop, so the water works show. It replaces the 5 m terrain lattice here (147 lattice quads cut) and subsides with the meadow.

parts.name: Molenerf with the screw trench, race and voorwaterloop
parts.desc: The ground round the mill at 1-2 m (0.5 m by the mill) with wall-aligned cuts for the race, the wheel pit, the screw trench and the board-lined voorwaterloop, so the water works show. It replaces the 5 m terrain lattice here (147 lattice quads cut) and subsides with the meadow.

parts.name: Molenerf today (outfall filled)
parts.desc: The ground round the mill at 1-2 m (0.5 m by the mill) with wall-aligned cuts for the race, the wheel pit, the screw trench and the board-lined voorwaterloop, so the water works show. It replaces the 5 m terrain lattice here (147 lattice quads cut) and subsides with the meadow.

parts.name: Voorwaterloop (outfall canal) water
parts.desc: Polder water lifted by the mill stands here at boezem level, about 1.8 m above the molentocht, between board-revetted banks and low kades, and runs about 150 m west to a culvert under the Binnenweg dike into the Amstel. Photo 28 shows it brim-full beside the mill.

parts.name: Voorwaterloop board revetment and kades
parts.desc: Planks behind round piles hold the canal banks (photo 28). The kades either side stand about half a metre above the water.

parts.name: Culvert head and sluice gate (schuif)
parts.desc: Where the voorwaterloop meets the Binnenweg dike it dives into a brick culvert under the road to the Amstel; a wooden sliding gate (schuif) in grooves can close it.

parts.name: Outfall on the Amstel (flap doors)
parts.desc: The culvert under the Binnenweg ends in the Amstel bank behind two hinged oak flap doors (klepdeuren) that the outflow pushes open and the river presses shut.

specs.Doors: 2 x 0.8 x 1.2 m oak, hinged at the top

parts.name: Plank footbridge over the voorwaterloop
parts.desc: A white-railed plank bridge crosses the outfall right in front of the mill (photos 29 and 30).

specs.Deck: 1.2 m, oak planks on two beams

parts.name: Timber wheel race (wipmolen)
parts.desc: Plank-and-pile race walls carry the wipmolen's 5 m scoop wheel; the floor rises under the wheel as the opleider (breast) so the paddles push water up and over the sill.

parts.name: Race water
parts.desc: Polder water at the molentocht end of the race, boezem water past the sill.

parts.name: Wachtdeur (check door)
parts.desc: A heavy door hung from the top just past the sill: the water thrown over the breast pushes it open, and when the wheel stops the higher boezem water slams it shut so the polder does not flood back.

parts.name: Krooshek (weed screen)
parts.desc: Slanted iron bars on an oak beam keep duckweed, reed and ice out of the wheel race.

parts.name: Brick wheel race: krimpmuren and opleider
parts.desc: The scoop wheel turns between two brick krimpmuren. Its paddles drag polder water from the molentocht up the curved brick opleider and over the sill into the voorwaterloop; the wachtdeur then swings shut against back-flow. Brick races replaced timber in the 19th century (De Zwaan's in 1888).

parts.name: Race water
parts.desc: Polder water at the molentocht end of the race, boezem water past the sill.

parts.name: Wachtdeur (check door)
parts.desc: A heavy door hung from the top just past the sill: the water thrown over the breast pushes it open, and when the wheel stops the higher boezem water slams it shut so the polder does not flood back.

parts.name: Krooshek (weed screen)
parts.desc: Slanted iron bars on an oak beam keep duckweed, reed and ice out of the wheel race.

parts.name: Outfall race from the screw's stortebak
parts.desc: After 1893 only the west end of the old race stays: the water the screw lifts into the stortebak inside the base runs out under the floor through the old wateras opening.

parts.name: Race water
parts.desc: Polder water at the molentocht end of the race, boezem water past the sill.

parts.name: Brick base (veldmuren)
parts.desc: The one-storey octagonal brick base on which the thatched body stands: the miller's living floor with door and windows, and below it the wheel pit. It survived the fire of 1921 and still carries today's house on Binnenweg 22.

parts.desc: A ledged door and small-paned windows in the base: the miller and his family lived here. Woodwork dark green with white frames, as on De Zwaan.

parts.name: Octagon frame: corner posts and veldkruisen
parts.desc: Eight oak achtkantstijlen lean in from the brick base to the curb; each face is stiffened by a veldkruis (St Andrew's cross) and horizontal regels; floor beams (bintlagen) with knee braces tie the posts together. De Zwaan has the same 'eiken achtkant'.

parts.name: Floors (zolders) and stairs
parts.desc: The miller's family lived on the ground floor inside the brick base; above it plank zolders on the bintlagen and steep ladder-stairs lead up to the cap. Every floor has an opening for the upright shaft.

parts.name: Cap (kap), thatched
parts.desc: The turning cap: reed thatch on curved cap rafters (kapspanten), rounded at the back, open at the front for the windshaft. It turns on the curb to keep the sails in the wind.

parts.name: Cap front and baard
parts.desc: The boarded front of the cap with the baard, the decorative board under the windshaft: dark green with white trim like De Zwaan's.

specs.Baard: 3.4 x 0.75 m, dark green, white trim

parts.name: Cap frame: windpeluw, penbalk, bearings
parts.desc: The heavy oak frame of the cap: two voeghouten sliding on the curb rollers, the windpeluw (breast beam) carrying the neck bearing (halslager, stone/bronze) and the penbalk with the tail bearing (penlager) that takes the thrust; the sprijzel holds the top of the upright shaft.

parts.name: Curb (kruiwerk) ring
parts.desc: The oak curb on top of the octagon with its iron track: the cap rides on it.

parts.name: Curb rollers (rollenkruiwerk, 47)
parts.desc: 47 iron rollers in a ring between the curb and the cap (De Zwaan has 47): the cap rolls round on them when the miller winds it.

parts.name: Windshaft (bovenas), oak
parts.desc: The original oak windshaft: a squared trunk with iron bands and a mortised head for the two stocks.

parts.name: Windshaft (bovenas), cast iron
parts.desc: A cast-iron windshaft with its poll end (askop), typical after c.1850 (the Riekermolen's is 1862).

parts.name: Poll end (askop)
parts.desc: The cast-iron head of the windshaft with two sockets (roe-gaten) for the inner and outer stock.

parts.name: Brake wheel (bovenwiel), 49 cogs
parts.desc: The big face wheel on the windshaft: elm rim with 49 hardwood kammen (cogs) facing backwards onto the lantern below. The Flemish brake clamps its rim.

parts.name: Flemish brake (Vlaamse vang)
parts.desc: Five poplar brake blocks (vangstukken) linked by iron straps wrap the brake-wheel rim. Pulling the brake lever down clamps them; lifting it frees the sails.

parts.name: Brake lever (vangstok) and vangtouw
parts.desc: The long brake lever sticks out of the side of the cap; a rope (vangtouw) hangs from it to the ground so the miller can stop the mill. Its state is the viewer's brake control.

parts.name: Wallower (bovenschijfloop), 24 staves
parts.desc: The lantern pinion at the top of the upright shaft: two oak discs joined by 24 staves that the brake wheel's cogs push round, about twice as fast as the sails.

parts.name: Upright shaft (koningsspil)
parts.desc: The tall 16-sided pine upright shaft carries the power from the cap down to the water machinery, standing on a bronze footstep (taatspot) on the spilkalf.

parts.name: Lower lantern (onderschijfloop), 20 staves
parts.desc: At the foot of the upright shaft a second lantern drives the pit wheel.

parts.name: Pit wheel (onderwiel), 73 cogs
parts.desc: The big vertical face wheel on the water shaft, half sunk in the wheel pit, turned by the lower lantern: here the speed drops to about 13 rpm for the scoop wheel.

parts.name: Water shaft (wateras), oak
parts.desc: The horizontal shaft from the pit wheel through the north wall to the scoop wheel, carried by the binnenlager in the pit and the buitenlager in the waterstoel of the race wall.

parts.name: Water shaft (wateras), cast iron
parts.desc: The horizontal shaft from the pit wheel through the north wall to the scoop wheel, carried by the binnenlager in the pit and the buitenlager in the waterstoel of the race wall.

parts.name: Scoop wheel (scheprad), wooden
parts.desc: Ø 5.6 m x 0.50 m with 24 paddles set tangent to the afschotcirkel (1/8 of the diameter) so they leave the water cleanly. Wooden: kruisarmen through the oak shaft, felloes and oak paddles.

parts.name: Scoop wheel (scheprad), iron
parts.desc: Ø 5.6 m x 0.50 m with 24 paddles set tangent to the afschotcirkel (1/8 of the diameter) so they leave the water cleanly. Iron: a cast-iron hub (sintelstuk) with schoepveren, rings and wooden paddles, like the Loenderveense mill's.

parts.name: Pit bearings, spilkalf and wheel housing
parts.desc: The draagbalk with the inner bearing of the water shaft, the spilkalf with the footstep of the upright shaft, the outer bearing in the race wall, and the boarded housing over the scoop wheel.

parts.name: Bevel gear (onderbonkelaar), 30 cogs
parts.desc: From 1893 a wooden bevel gear at the foot of the upright shaft drives the screw.

parts.name: Screw gear (vijzelwiel), 39 cogs
parts.desc: The crown-like wooden gear on top of the screw's beam, meshing with the onderbonkelaar (photo 24).

parts.name: Archimedean screw (vijzel)
parts.desc: Fitted in 1893 by W. Kool of Moordrecht: a wooden beam with three steel screw threads, Ø 1.7 m, lying at about 30 deg in a brick trough (kom). Turning at ~38 rpm it lifts polder water up to the stortebak inside the base; a screw can lift 4-5 m where a scoop wheel manages 1.5. During the work millwright A.J. Hazenbosch (56) fell to his death on 24 July 1893.

parts.name: Spilkalf (screw period)
parts.desc: The footstep beam of the upright shaft, turned north-south in 1893 to clear the screw gear.

parts.name: Screw trough (vijzelkom), stortebak and achterwaterloop
parts.desc: The brick half-cylinder trough the screw turns in, the stortebak at its top inside the base where the lifted water spills out, the retaining walls of the screw trench and the achterwaterloop from the molentocht. After 1922 the trench served the electric pump as its suction pit.

parts.name: Water in the screw trench and stortebak
parts.desc: Polder water fills the trench and the lower part of the trough; lifted water in the stortebak.

parts.name: Screw housing
parts.desc: A tarred plank housing over the upper part of the screw outside the base keeps out frost and children.

parts.name: Inner stock (binnenroede), pitch pine
parts.desc: A tapering pitch-pine stock, iron-banded, through the head of the windshaft.

parts.name: Outer stock (buitenroede), pitch pine
parts.desc: A tapering pitch-pine stock, iron-banded, through the head of the windshaft.

parts.name: Inner stock (binnenroede), riveted iron
parts.desc: Riveted iron stock by Pot, fitted 1882/83: the vlucht measured 23.10 m in 1864 and 23.20 m in 1894.

parts.name: Outer stock (buitenroede), riveted iron
parts.desc: Riveted iron stock by Pot, fitted 1882/83: the vlucht measured 23.10 m in 1864 and 23.20 m in 1894.

parts.name: Sail lattice (hekwerk) 1
parts.desc: Oud-Hollands sail frame: about 22 heklatten through the stock, the hekstijlen and voorzoom, and white windborden on the leading edge; twisted from ~17 deg at the hub to ~4 deg at the tip (zeeg).

parts.name: Sail cloth 1 (set)
parts.desc: Flax/cotton canvas spread over the lattice and tied off; the miller reefs it in four positions for the wind.

parts.desc: The same cloths rolled up and tied along the frames, as when the mill stands still. Shown by the viewer's sail state instead of the set cloths.

parts.name: Tail (staart), struts and ladder
parts.desc: The long tail beam with its two struts (schoren) runs from the back of the cap down to the ground; the ladder beside it is the miller's way up to the cap (photos 29, 30). The whole cap turns with it.

parts.name: Winding wheel (kruirad)
parts.desc: An eight-spoked oak wheel on the foot of the tail. Turning it winds the chain to a kruipaal and pulls the cap, sails and tail round into the wind (photo 09).

parts.name: Winding posts (kruipalen)
parts.desc: A ring of oak posts round the mill: the winding chain is hooked to the post in the right direction and the kruirad pulls the cap round to it.

parts.name: Brick footing (veldmuren)
parts.desc: A low square brick footing with a slot for the water shaft carries the ondertoren.

parts.name: Lower body (ondertoren), thatched
parts.desc: The pyramid-shaped lower body: four corner posts (hoekstijlen) and braces round the hollow post, thatched with reed (photo 11 shows the form).

parts.name: Hollow post (koker) and onderzetel
parts.desc: The square hollow post of planks on four kokerstijlen: the upright shaft runs inside it, and the cap-house turns round it on the wooden seats (zetelkruiwerk).

parts.name: Cap-house (bovenhuis) with barrel roof
parts.desc: The box-shaped cap-house sits on the bovenzetel and turns with sails and tail: dark-green boarding (kleedhout) on the stormbint, side binten and trapbint, under a barrel roof.

parts.name: Windshaft (bovenas), oak
parts.desc: An oak windshaft through the stormbint, with the stock mortises in its head.

parts.name: Brake wheel (bovenwiel), 41 cogs
parts.desc: The wipmolen's smaller brake wheel (cog counts unrecorded; estimated).

parts.name: Upright shaft with both lanterns
parts.desc: The koningsspil runs down inside the hollow post: a 21-stave lantern at the top, a 19-stave lantern at the foot driving the pit wheel.

parts.name: Pit wheel (waterwiel), 61 cogs
parts.desc: The pit wheel on the water shaft under the ondertoren.

parts.name: Water shaft (wateras), oak
parts.desc: Oak water shaft with iron bands to the 5 m scoop wheel.

parts.desc: Ø 5.0 m x 0.40 m with 20 paddles set tangent to the afschotcirkel (1/8 of the diameter) so they leave the water cleanly. Wooden: kruisarmen through the oak shaft, felloes and oak paddles.

parts.name: Pit bearings and spil footstep (wipmolen)
parts.desc: Draagbalk, footstep beam and the outer bearing post.

parts.name: Stocks (roeden), wooden
parts.desc: Two tapering wooden stocks for a ~22 m gevlucht.

parts.name: Sail lattices and cloths (wipmolen)
parts.desc: Four Oud-Hollands sails with their cloths set.

parts.desc: The long tail beam with its two struts (schoren) runs from the back of the cap down to the ground; the ladder beside it is the miller's way up to the cap (photos 29, 30). The whole cap turns with it.
